edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 128 opens with a beatitude, “Blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh, who walks in his ways.” (web:Ps.128.0 = oshb:Ps.128.1; the title שִׁ֗יר הַֽמַּ֫עֲל֥וֹת carries no ascription). Second-person address to the man begins already at web:Ps.128.2 (oshb:Ps.128.2: יְגִ֣יעַ כַּ֭פֶּיךָ, 'your hands'; תֹאכֵ֑ל, 'you will eat') and continues through web:Ps.128.3 (oshb:Ps.128.3: אֶשְׁתְּךָ֤, 'your wife'; בָּ֭נֶיךָ, 'your children'), before the psalm gathers this household description back into third person at its own summary, “Behold, this is how the man who fears Yahweh is blessed.” (web:Ps.128.4). The direct blessing that follows, “May Yahweh bless you out of Zion...” (web:Ps.128.5), closing “...Peace be upon Israel.” (web:Ps.128.6), continues the same second-person address already open since 128:2 rather than opening it. The psalm's real shape is a third-person beatitude frame at web:Ps.128.1 and web:Ps.128.4 enclosing continuous second-person address from web:Ps.128.2 through web:Ps.128.6, so the six verses stand as one composition.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.128.4/web:Ps.128.5 was considered but rejected: second-person address to the man does not first appear at web:Ps.128.5 -- it already runs through web:Ps.128.2-web:Ps.128.3 -- so no third-person/second-person split exists at that seam to divide on. The psalm's actual frame (third person at web:Ps.128.1 and web:Ps.128.4 enclosing second-person address at web:Ps.128.2-web:Ps.128.3 and web:Ps.128.5-web:Ps.128.6) supports unity more strongly than a division at 4/5 would.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person suffixed forms open already at oshb:Ps.128.2 (יְגִ֣יעַ כַּ֭פֶּיךָ 'your hands', תֹאכֵ֑ל 'you will eat') and oshb:Ps.128.3 (אֶשְׁתְּךָ֤ 'your wife', בָּ֭נֶיךָ 'your children'), byte tier, continuous through web:Ps.128.5-web:Ps.128.6; third person frames the second-person material only at web:Ps.128.1 and web:Ps.128.4

the closing formula שָׁ֝ל֗וֹם עַל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (oshb:Ps.128.6, byte tier, 'peace be on Israel') is byte-identical (3 of 3 words match) to the closing formula of Psalm 125 (oshb:Ps.125.5), a shared liturgical tag disclosed as texture, not a merge
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 128 stands complete in itself as one composition, its parent grouping simply Psalm 128.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 129 opens “A Song of Ascents.” (web:Ps.129.0 = oshb:Ps.129.1, שִׁ֗יר הַֽמַּ֫עֲל֥וֹת, byte tier) before the summons יֹֽאמַר נָ֝א יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (oshb:Ps.129.1, byte tier, 'let Israel now say') — the same clause that closes 124:1 — introduces a complaint repeated almost word for word at its own start, “Many times they have afflicted me from my youth up.” (web:Ps.129.1-web:Ps.129.2). The plowing metaphor of web:Ps.129.3 develops the affliction, Yahweh's justice answers it at web:Ps.129.4, and an extended curse against 'those who hate Zion' runs from web:Ps.129.5 through the closing negative blessing, “Neither do those who go by say...” (web:Ps.129.8), withholding the greeting the psalm's opponents would otherwise receive. The repeated opening line binds web:Ps.129.1-web:Ps.129.2 as one unit rather than two, and from web:Ps.129.3 through web:Ps.129.8, 0 of 6 verses name a party distinct from 'the wicked' (129:4) or 'those who hate Zion' (129:5); the complaint does turn from a qatal report (129:1-4) to a jussive curse beginning at 129:5, but the referent stays the same across that turn, so the whole eight-verse psalm holds as one row.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.129.2/web:Ps.129.3, following the repeated opening line, was considered but rejected because the repetition is an intensifying doubling of one complaint rather than a formal envelope closing off a separate unit.
observed_substrate_signals: רַ֭בַּת צְרָר֣וּנִי מִנְּעוּרַ֑י (oshb:Ps.129.1) and רַ֭בַּת צְרָר֣וּנִי מִנְּעוּרָ֑י (oshb:Ps.129.2) share the same three-word skeleton, רבת צררוני מנעורי (skeleton tier, 3 of 3 words), differing at the byte tier in the final word's suffix vowel alone — the same consonantal repetition the part's step-parallelism texture elsewhere shows
web:Ps.129.3 crosses a ketiv/qere pair — ketiv למענותם against the qere לְמַעֲנִיתָֽם (oshb:Ps.129.3, pmarks_Ps.json kq) — a scribal correction that does not touch this row's boundary
edited_rows.device_notes: A single parent, Psalm 129, holds this psalm's one row.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 130 opens “A Song of Ascents.” (web:Ps.130.0 = oshb:Ps.130.1, שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּעֲל֑וֹת, byte tier) before the psalmist's own cry, “Out of the depths I have cried to you, Yahweh.” (web:Ps.130.1), and the plea for a hearing that follows (web:Ps.130.2). A rhetorical question about surviving Yahweh's record of sins (web:Ps.130.3) is answered by the confession “But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared.” (web:Ps.130.4), and the voice continues in the first person through a waiting confession, “I wait for Yahweh. My soul waits. I hope in his word.” (web:Ps.130.5), intensified by the watchmen simile at web:Ps.130.6. Across these six verses the name Israel does not occur -- though oshb:Ps.130.6 does name 'watchmen' twice inside the span (0 of 6 verses at the skeleton tier); 'Israel' — the addressee of the psalm's remaining two verses — has not yet appeared, so the personal cry, confession, and waiting form one unit before the corporate turn.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A whole-psalm reading of Psalm 130's eight verses was considered, since the part's short psalms default to one row, but rejected because a genuine addressee shift — from the psalmist's own first-person cry and confession to an imperative summons naming 'Israel', unmentioned in the preceding six verses — opens at web:Ps.130.7, strong enough to divide even this short a psalm.
observed_substrate_signals: the name Israel does not occur anywhere in web:Ps.130.1-web:Ps.130.6 at the skeleton tier (0 of 6 verses); it occurs in both remaining verses, web:Ps.130.7 and web:Ps.130.8 (2 of 2), a sweep-confirmed split at the 6|7 seam

מִשֹּׁמְרִ֥ים לַ֝בֹּ֗קֶר שֹׁמְרִ֥ים לַבֹּֽקֶר (oshb:Ps.130.6, byte tier, 'more than watchmen long for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning') doubles its own noun rather than introducing a new addressee, keeping web:Ps.130.6 inside the psalmist's own first-person voice
edited_rows.device_notes: Both rows of Psalm 130 share one parent — the composition as a whole.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 131's title names David, “A Song of Ascents. By David.” (web:Ps.131.0 = oshb:Ps.131.1, שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּֽעֲל֗וֹת לְדָ֫וִ֥ד, byte tier), the part's third such ascription. The body is one humility confession addressed to Yahweh, “Yahweh, my heart isn't arrogant, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me.” (web:Ps.131.1), developed by the weaned-child simile of web:Ps.131.2, and closed by the same imperative summons that ends Psalm 130, “Israel, hope in Yahweh, from this time forward and forever more.” (web:Ps.131.3). At three verses — the fewest of the 15 ascents together with Psalms 133 and 134 — the confession, its simile, and the closing summons to Israel form one uninterrupted movement with no internal address change strong enough to divide it.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.131.2/web:Ps.131.3, separating the psalmist's own confession from the closing summons to Israel, was considered but rejected because three verses is too short to support a formal division and the summons functions as the confession's own resolution rather than a new topic.
observed_substrate_signals: superscription cite: web:Ps.131.0 = oshb:Ps.131.1 and carries לְדָ֫וִ֥ד (oshb:Ps.131.1, byte tier), the part's third le-David ascent title (sweep: 12 titled psalms, 3 le-David: 122, 124, 131)
כְּ֭גָמֻל עֲלֵ֣י אִמּ֑וֹ (oshb:Ps.131.2, byte tier, 'like a weaned child with his mother') is this psalm's own simile, not shared with any other psalm in the part

יַחֵ֣ל יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל אֶל יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.131.3, byte tier) closes the part's psalms on the same summons that opens Psalm 130's second movement (oshb:Ps.130.7), an accent-stripped-tier match disclosed as texture
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 131's row belongs to one parent unit spanning the whole composition.

edited_rows.rationale: The community's own recollection follows David's oath: an unquoted report “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah. We found it in the field of Jaar.” (web:Ps.132.6) gives way to a quoted communal vow, “We will go into his dwelling place. We will worship at his footstool.” (web:Ps.132.7), then to unquoted imperative address to Yahweh: “קוּמָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה לִמְנוּחָתֶ֑ךָ” (oshb:Ps.132.8) -- “Arise, Yahweh, into your resting place,” (web:Ps.132.8) -- continuing through the petition “For your servant David's sake, don't turn away the face of your anointed one.” (web:Ps.132.10). The row groups the search-recollection, the processional vow, and the petition as one liturgical movement; grammatical address turns from third person at web:Ps.132.6-web:Ps.132.7 (oshb:Ps.132.7: נִ֝שְׁתַּחֲוֶ֗ה לַהֲדֹ֥ם רַגְלָֽיו, 'we will worship at his footstool') to second-person vocative address to Yahweh beginning at web:Ps.132.8 (קוּמָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה, 'arise, Yahweh'), but no fresh narrative report clause comparable to 132:6's own opening intervenes before the next report opens at web:Ps.132.11, so the movement holds as one row: it opens where the quoted vow of 132:3-132:5 closes and ends where that next report opens at web:Ps.132.11.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the vow (132:6-7) from the petition (132:8-10) was considered, since 132:8 drops the quotation marks that bound 132:7 and turns from third-person description to second-person address; rejected because no fresh narrative report clause comparable to 132:6's own opening intervenes before 132:11's own next report -- 132:8's imperative-plus-vocative continues the same movement's action rather than opening a fresh report.
observed_substrate_signals: quotation-marked communal vow at web:Ps.132.7, bounded by unquoted material on both sides (132:6, 132:8)
second-person imperative address to Yahweh begins at web:Ps.132.8 and continues without a fresh vocative through web:Ps.132.10
no selah occurs anywhere in this row's own span, web:Ps.132.6-web:Ps.132.10, per the pmarks_Ps.json inventory (the absence claim is scoped strictly to that span)

edited_rows.rationale: A reciprocal oath answers David's: “נִשְׁבַּֽע יְהוָ֨ה לְדָוִ֡ד אֱמֶת֮” (oshb:Ps.132.11) -- “Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it:” (web:Ps.132.11) -- opens a quotation mid-verse, after this reporting clause, that runs through web:Ps.132.12's own final character (“…their children also will sit on your throne forever more.”), reusing at the skeleton tier the same swearing-verb root that opened the report at oshb:Ps.132.2 (נִ֭שְׁבַּע). web:Ps.132.13 then drops the quotation and reports, in the third person, “For Yahweh has chosen Zion. He has desired it for his habitation.” -- a motive clause that names the ground of the oath just sworn and supplies the only naming of Zion that the following oracle's web:Ps.132.15-web:Ps.132.17 (outside this row's own span) depend on grammatically, and sets up the first-person oracle quotation that opens immediately after it at web:Ps.132.14. The two-word phrase עֲדֵי עַ֑ד ('forever and ever') stands byte-identically (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12 and oshb:Ps.132.14, straddling this row's own closing seam without moving it. The row closes at 132:13 rather than carrying the motive clause into the following quotation.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching 132:13 to the following oracle (132:14-18) instead was considered, since both concern Zion's election; rejected here because 132:13 stays in third-person report while 132:14 opens a first-person quotation of Yahweh's own voice -- the stronger, quotation-marked seam sits at 132:13|14, not 132:12|13.
observed_substrate_signals: the oath-verb forms at oshb:Ps.132.2 (נִ֭שְׁבַּע) and oshb:Ps.132.11 (נִשְׁבַּֽע) match at skeleton tier only (byte=False, accent_stripped=False since 132:11 retains a meteg absent from 132:2); not claimed to govern the whole row

the quotation opens mid-132:11, after the reporting clause, not at that verse's first character; it closes at web:Ps.132.12's own final character, not mid-verse; 132:13 is unquoted third-person report
no selah in Ps.132.11-Ps.132.13 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

132:13 supplies the only naming of Zion that the following oracle's web:Ps.132.15-web:Ps.132.17 (outside this row's own span) depend on grammatically; the two-word phrase עֲדֵי עַ֑ד ('forever and ever') repeats byte-identically (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12 and oshb:Ps.132.14, straddling this row's own 132:13|14 seam without moving it

edited_rows.rationale: A first-person divine oracle opens “זֹאת מְנוּחָתִ֥י עֲדֵי עַ֑ד” (oshb:Ps.132.14) -- “This is my resting place forever. I will live here, for I have desired it.” (web:Ps.132.14) -- and runs in Yahweh's own voice through the psalm's close, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but on himself, his crown will shine.” (web:Ps.132.18), where the quotation mark shuts with the psalm. The oracle promises Zion's provision (132:15), her priests' salvation (132:16), David's horn and lamp (132:17), and his enemies' shame against his own shining crown (132:18). The oracle's Zion-provision promise (132:15-132:17) depends grammatically on the antecedent Zion named once, at web:Ps.132.13, one verse outside this row's own span. The two-word phrase עֲדֵי עַ֑ד that opens this row's own quotation at 132:14 also stands byte-identically (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12, in the preceding oath quotation, straddling this row's opening seam without moving it: the third-person-to-first-person voice pivot at 132:13|14 remains the stronger driver. This is the Zion-election oracle proper, distinct from 132:13's third-person report of the same election.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 132:13, where Zion's election is initially named, was considered; rejected because 132:13 is third-person narration while 132:14 is the oracle's own first-person voice, marked by the WEB quotation boundary.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person divine quotation opens web:Ps.132.14 and closes at the psalm's own end, web:Ps.132.18 (WEB quotation marks)
no selah in Ps.132.14-Ps.132.18 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)
עֲדֵי עַ֑ד ('forever and ever') is byte-identical (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12 and oshb:Ps.132.14 (this row's own opening word), straddling the 132:13|14 seam without moving it

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 134's title repeats 132's own wording, bare shir hamma'alot with no name attached (web:Ps.134.0 = oshb:Ps.134.1). Its three verses form one antiphonal exchange: an imperative call to the night-watch temple servants, “Look! Praise Yahweh, all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house!” (web:Ps.134.1), continuing “Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.134.2), (בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Ps.134.1, the imperative 'bless Yahweh', which WEB renders 'praise'; וּ֝בָרֲכוּ אֶת יְהוָֽה, oshb:Ps.134.2, the same 2mp imperative repeated), then a reply that reverses the direction of blessing: “יְבָרֶכְךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה מִצִּיּ֑וֹן” (oshb:Ps.134.3) -- “May Yahweh bless you from Zion, even he who made heaven and earth.” (web:Ps.134.3). The same root now stands 3ms with a 2ms object suffix ('he will bless you'). The call (134:1-2) addresses the servants in the imperative; the reply (134:3) turns the blessing back onto whoever has just spoken it, closing the short ascents collection's coda with this exchange rather than a further imperative.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating 134:1-2 and 134:3 as two rows was considered, since the addressee reverses between them (servants addressed, then the worshipper blessed); rejected because three verses is too little to divide without padding, and no vocative, quotation, or report boundary marks an independent seam between the call and its answer.
observed_substrate_signals: title: shir hamma'alot, no name label (as 132, against 133's le-David; oshb:Ps.134.1)
second-person imperative addressee ("you" plural, the servants) in 134:1-2 reverses to second-person singular blessing-recipient in 134:3
no selah in Ps.134 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence, whole psalm)

the blessing root appears 3 times: 2mp imperative at oshb:Ps.134.1 (בָּרֲכ֣וּ) and oshb:Ps.134.2 (וּ֝בָרֲכוּ), then 3ms-with-2ms-suffix at oshb:Ps.134.3 (יְבָרֶכְךָ֣) -- the imperative call is answered in the same root, reversed in direction
edited_rows.device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition: parent grouping Psalm 134, whole and undivided.

edited_rows.rationale: Untitled, Psalm 135 opens “הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ הַֽ֭לְלוּ אֶת שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.1) -- “Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh's name! Praise him, you servants of Yahweh,” (web:Ps.135.1) -- an imperative call to praise that continues through web:Ps.135.3's own hallelu-Yah (“Praise Yah, for Yahweh is good. Sing praises to his name, for that is pleasant.”), then supplies an opening motive for praise, “For Yah has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession.” (web:Ps.135.4). The psalm's hallelu-Yah frame opens here in both its occurrences (verse-initial at 135:1 and 135:3, per psalm_device_inventory.json's halleluyah inventory) and, on that inventory, recurs verse-finally at the psalm's own close -- a frame this opening row does not itself carry evidence for past its own span.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending the row at 135:3, keeping just the imperative praise-calls together, was considered and is a serious rival reading. The particle "for" that opens both 135:4 and 135:5 stands on both sides of the 4|5 seam and is absent from 135:3's own opening, so it cannot itself be the reason a seam falls at 3|4 rather than 4|5 -- as a shared particle it argues for extending the rival span through 135:4, not against it. The stronger reason to keep 135:4 with this row instead is 135:5's own first-person-singular opening (oshb:Ps.135.5: כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י, 'for I'), which launches an eight-verse third-person-dominant unit that 135:4's own motive clause does not share.
observed_substrate_signals: hallelu-Yah verse-initial at web:Ps.135.1 and web:Ps.135.3 (psalm_device_inventory.json halleluyah.verse_initial; 2 of the book's 11 verse-initial occurrences fall in this span)
motive-clause particle "for" opens both 135:4 and the following verse 135:5, a lexical bridge across this row's own closing seam
edited_rows.device_notes: One parent, Psalm 135, spans every row below it.

edited_rows.rationale: “כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי כִּי גָד֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.5) -- “For I know that Yahweh is great, that our Lord is above all gods.” (web:Ps.135.5) -- opens a declarative unit that runs through creation (“Whatever Yahweh pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth,” web:Ps.135.6; the clouds, lightning, and wind of web:Ps.135.7) into historical recital: “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and animal.” (web:Ps.135.8), signs and wonders sent on Pharaoh (web:Ps.135.9), many nations and mighty kings struck (web:Ps.135.10), “Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan-” (web:Ps.135.11), and their land given as a heritage to Israel (web:Ps.135.12). 135:5 itself is first-person (כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי, 'for I know', the row's own opening quote) and web:Ps.135.9 addresses Egypt directly in the second-person feminine singular (oshb:Ps.135.9: בְּתוֹכֵ֣כִי מִצְרָ֑יִם, 'in your midst, Egypt'); third-person description of Yahweh's own acts otherwise holds across 6 of 8 verses (135:6,7,8,10,11,12). The row closes where the psalm's address turns from Egypt (135:9) to Yahweh by name at web:Ps.135.13 (“Your name, Yahweh, endures forever”) -- an addressee-identity shift, not a person-number one, since 135:9 already carries second-person address inside this row's own span.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting creation (135:5-7) from the historical recital (135:8-12) was considered; rejected because no vocative, quotation, or addressee change marks that content transition -- Yahweh remains the third-person grammatical subject throughout, even where 135:9 addresses Egypt directly in the second person as the object of his acts.
observed_substrate_signals: third-person description of Yahweh's acts holds across 6 of 8 verses (135:6,7,8,10,11,12); 135:5 opens first-person (oshb:Ps.135.5: כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי) and 135:9 addresses Egypt in the second-person feminine singular (oshb:Ps.135.9: בְּתוֹכֵ֣כִי מִצְרָ֑יִם, 'in your midst, Egypt')

second-person address continues at web:Ps.135.13, now naming Yahweh rather than Egypt -- an addressee-identity shift, not a first appearance of second person, since 135:9 already addresses Egypt in second person within this row's own span

edited_rows.rationale: “יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְךָ֣ לְעוֹלָ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.135.13) -- “Your name, Yahweh, endures forever; your renown, Yahweh, throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.135.13) -- turns briefly to direct second-person address of Yahweh, naming him twice by vocative; web:Ps.135.14 then reverts to third person, “For Yahweh will judge his people and have compassion on his servants.” Both of 135:14's own verbs (oshb:Ps.135.14: יָדִ֣ין, יִתְנֶחָֽם) are prefix-conjugation forms, distinct from the suffix-conjugation forms that open the historical recital's own verses (135:8, 135:10). This two-verse span sits as a hinge between the historical recital closing at 135:12 and the idol polemic opening at 135:15: it neither continues the third-person recital's unbroken run nor opens the polemic's own topic.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching this couplet to the preceding historical recital (135:5-12) was considered and rejected for the second-person vocative that opens 135:13; attaching it to the idol polemic that follows (135:15-18) was also considered and rejected because 135:14 names Yahweh's compassion on his own people, not yet the idols' impotence that 135:15 begins.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person vocative address to Yahweh ("Yahweh" named twice) opens web:Ps.135.13, unlike the third person on both sides of this span

edited_rows.rationale: “עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב” (oshb:Ps.135.15) -- “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.” (web:Ps.135.15) -- opens an idol polemic that runs through mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see (web:Ps.135.16), ears that cannot hear (web:Ps.135.17), to the closing verdict, “Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.” (web:Ps.135.18). This four-verse unit shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 115's idol polemic (115:4-115:8): a word-by-word byte comparison of both psalms' own text (verse_map_oshb.json) finds oshb:Ps.135.16 matching oshb:Ps.115.5 and oshb:Ps.135.18 matching oshb:Ps.115.8 letter-for-letter, while 135:15's construct chain with the article (עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם) differs from 115:4's suffixed plural (oshb:Ps.115.4: עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם), and 135:17's own clause (oshb:Ps.135.17: אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ) is longer than 115:6 alone on all 3 measures taken (skeleton words, consonants, codepoints), running shorter only against 115:6-115:7 combined, and substitutes a different verb root (יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ for oshb:Ps.115.6's יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) inside the clause the two verses share. It is discussed here as a recognizable, recurring cross-psalm texture, not merged with Ps 115's own rows.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 135:14 instead, to fold in Yahweh's compassion as a foil to the idols' impotence, was considered; kept separate because 135:14's two verbs (oshb:Ps.135.14: יָדִ֣ין, יִתְנֶחָֽם) are prefix-conjugation forms belonging with 135:13 in a distinct hinge couplet, not the suffix-conjugation forms of the historical recital (135:8, 135:10) -- and 135:14 does not yet reach the idols' inertness that 135:15 introduces as a fresh topic either way.

edited_rows.rationale: A fourfold bless-call opens “בֵּ֣ית יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.19) -- “House of Israel, praise Yahweh! House of Aaron, praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.135.19) -- and continues “בֵּ֣ית הַ֭לֵּוִי בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.20) -- “House of Levi, praise Yahweh! You who fear Yahweh, praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.135.20). Four addressee groups are named across these two verses (house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, those who fear Yahweh); comparison against Ps 115's own trust-call (Israel, house of Aaron, those who fear Yahweh, named at 115:9-11) and Ps 118's own call-and-response (the same three) finds both naming three groups where this psalm's own bless-call names four, adding house of Levi as a fourth member; Ps 115's own bless-call (115:12-13,18) opens instead with 'house of Israel', not bare 'Israel'. The imperative vocative form returns after the idol polemic, bracketing the psalm with its opening call, and web:Ps.135.21's closing benediction carries this psalm's own verse-final hallelu-Yah, “Blessed be Yahweh from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem. Praise Yah!”

edited_rows.rationale: Untitled, Psalm 136 opens “הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב” (oshb:Ps.136.1) -- “Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good,” (web:Ps.136.1) -- the verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH formula listed in psalm_device_inventory.json's hodu_openings (one of six book-wide, alongside 33:2, 105:1, 107:1, 118:1, 118:29). A triadic escalation follows: “Give thanks to the God of gods” (web:Ps.136.2), “Give thanks to the Lord of lords” (web:Ps.136.3), each closed by this psalm's own refrain. A verse-by-verse comparison of the refrain's own tail across all 26 verses of this psalm finds “כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ” (oshb:Ps.136.1) present in all 26, but not always in the same spelling: 136:3 spells the refrain's "forever" defectively, “לְעֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ” (oshb:Ps.136.3) (no vav in the second word), against the plene spelling in the other 25 -- an erratum-class spelling variant, not a break in the refrain's presence. web:Ps.136.4 then drops the imperative hodu-plus-object frame for a participial construction ("to him who…") that recurs through 136:4-25 but is interrupted by six finite-verb-headed verses (136:11,14,15,18,21,24), with the imperative hodu-plus-object frame itself returning at the psalm's own closing verse, 136:26 -- marking this row's own close at 136:3.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the row through 136:4 was considered, since 136:4's own participle still names an attribute of Yahweh; rejected because 136:1-3 share one grammatical frame (imperative hodu + direct object) that 136:4 replaces with a participial construction recurring through 136:4-25 (interrupted by six finite-verb verses: 136:11,14,15,18,21,24) before the imperative frame itself returns at the psalm's own close, 136:26.
observed_substrate_signals: hodu-le-YHWH verse-initial at web:Ps.136.1 (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings)

sweep: 26 of 26 verses in Ps 136 carry the closing refrain tail (direct verse-by-verse comparison of the final three words of each verse's own oshb text); 25 spelled plene, 1 (oshb:Ps.136.3) spelled defectively -- both attested spellings swept
grammatical frame shifts from imperative-plus-object (136:1-3) to participial construction beginning web:Ps.136.4
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 136's rows share a single parent composition throughout.

edited_rows.rationale: “לְעֹשֵׂ֣ה הַ֭שָּׁמַיִם בִּתְבוּנָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.136.5) -- “to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his loving kindness endures forever;” (web:Ps.136.5) -- opens the creation recital, continuing through the great wonders of web:Ps.136.4, the earth spread above the waters (web:Ps.136.6), the great lights (web:Ps.136.7), and their assignment to rule day and night (web:Ps.136.8-9). 4 of 6 verses (136:4,5,6,7) keep the participial "to him who…" construction; 136:8 and 136:9 open instead with the object marker, naming the sun/moon/stars as objects rather than repeating the participle, though all 6 close with this psalm's refrain. The row's content turns from cosmic creation to Israel's history at its own close, where web:Ps.136.10 turns to Egypt.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A seam within 136:4-9, separating the general "great wonders" of 136:4 from the specific creation acts of 136:5-9, was considered; rejected as no grammatical marker distinguishes 136:4 from what follows -- the span still forms one syntactic chain (136:8-9 continue it with the object marker rather than a fresh participle) under the psalm's own refrain.
observed_substrate_signals: the participial "to him who…" construction opens 4 of 6 verses (136:4,5,6,7); 136:8 and 136:9 continue the same syntactic chain with the object marker introducing their objects (the sun, the moon and stars) rather than repeating the participle -- one continuous chain, not a self-standing sentence break, across this book-wide seam
content turns from cosmic creation (136:4-9) to Egypt/exodus beginning web:Ps.136.10, without a grammatical-form change

edited_rows.rationale: The recital turns to the exodus: “to him who struck down the Egyptian firstborn,” (web:Ps.136.10), Israel brought out (web:Ps.136.11), with a strong hand and outstretched arm (web:Ps.136.12), the Red Sea divided (“לְגֹזֵ֣ר יַם ס֭וּף לִגְזָרִ֑ים” (oshb:Ps.136.13)), Israel passed through (web:Ps.136.14), and Pharaoh's army overthrown in the sea (web:Ps.136.15). All 6 verses in this span (136:10-15) close with this psalm's refrain, as do all 26 verses of this psalm. The row's content turns from the sea crossing to the wilderness march at its own close, where web:Ps.136.16 turns to the wilderness.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding 136:10 into the preceding creation row (136:4-9) was considered, since both share the participial frame; rejected because 136:10 is the recital's opening Egypt-naming verse, opening the exodus content movement rather than closing the creation one.
observed_substrate_signals: content moves from Egypt's plague (136:10) through the Red Sea crossing (136:13-15); grammatical form (participle/finite-verb alternation) does not itself mark this row's edges -- content alone does
wilderness march named beginning at web:Ps.136.16, immediately after this row's own close

edited_rows.rationale: The recital moves from wilderness to conquest: Yahweh led his people through the wilderness (web:Ps.136.16), struck great kings (web:Ps.136.17) and killed mighty kings (web:Ps.136.18), naming them by name -- “לְ֭סִיחוֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ הָאֱמֹרִ֑י” (oshb:Ps.136.19) (web:Ps.136.19) and “וּ֭לְעוֹג מֶ֣לֶךְ הַבָּשָׁ֑ן” (oshb:Ps.136.20) (web:Ps.136.20) -- before their land is given as a heritage to Israel (web:Ps.136.21-22). This Sihon/Og notice shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 135's own Sihon/Og verses (135:11-135:12): the Sihon clause (136:19 against 135:11) matches at the skeleton/accent-stripped tier only (differing in cantillation), the Og clause (136:20 against 135:11) is byte-identical, and the land-grant clause that follows (136:21-22 against 135:12) varies from Ps 135's own wording in two words at the skeleton/accent-stripped tier (four words differ at the byte tier, since two more carry accent-only differences). web:Ps.136.23 then shifts from third-person "his people" to first-person-plural "us", marking this row's own close.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the wilderness march (136:16) from the conquest naming (136:17-22) was considered; rejected because no grammatical or addressee change divides them -- both stay third-person description of Yahweh's acts toward "his people"/"Israel" under the shared refrain.
observed_substrate_signals: comparison against Ps 135's own Sihon/Og verses (135:11-135:12, verse_map_oshb.json): the Sihon clause (136:19) matches 135:11 at skeleton/accent-stripped tier only (cantillation differs); the Og clause (136:20) is byte-identical to 135:11; the land-grant clause (136:21-22) differs from 135:12 in two words at skeleton/accent-stripped tier, four words at byte tier -- cross-psalm texture, not a merged row
first-person-plural "us"/"our" opens immediately after this row's own close, at web:Ps.136.23

edited_rows.rationale: “שֶׁ֭בְּשִׁפְלֵנוּ זָ֣כַר לָ֑נוּ” (oshb:Ps.136.23) -- “who remembered us in our low estate,” (web:Ps.136.23) -- turns from the historical third person to first-person-plural address, continuing “and has delivered us from our adversaries,” (web:Ps.136.24) before web:Ps.136.25 widens to a universal, impersonal close, “who gives food to every creature,” before the psalm's own final verse returns to its opening imperative, “ה֭וֹדוּ לְאֵ֣ל הַשָּׁמָ֑יִם” (oshb:Ps.136.26) -- “Oh give thanks to the God of heaven,” (web:Ps.136.26) -- an inclusio repeating web:Ps.136.1's own hodu-le-YHWH opening imperative at the skeleton/accent-stripped tier (byte-identical to 136:2 and 136:3's own opening word, though not 136:1's, which differs only in cantillation); the divine-name member itself changes from 'Yahweh' (136:1) to 'the God of heaven' (136:26). The row closes the psalm at its own closing verse.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating 136:26 as its own one-verse coda, separate from 136:23-25, was considered for its inclusio function; rejected as too short to divide from the closing movement it caps, and the psalm's own refrain still binds it to 136:23-25 without a fresh addressee change.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person-plural "us"/"our" opens web:Ps.136.23, against the third-person "him"/"his" of all 19 verses from 136:4 through 136:22

web:Ps.136.26's opening word matches web:Ps.136.2 and web:Ps.136.3's own opening word at byte tier, and web:Ps.136.1's at skeleton/accent-stripped tier only (cantillation differs); the imperative itself forms the inclusio, though the following divine-name member changes from 'Yahweh' to 'the God of heaven'

edited_rows.rationale: Untitled, Psalm 137 opens “עַ֥ל נַהֲר֨וֹת בָּבֶ֗ל שָׁ֣ם יָ֭שַׁבְנוּ” (oshb:Ps.137.1) -- “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.” (web:Ps.137.1) -- a first-person-plural scene of captivity, continuing “On the willows in that land, we hung up our harps.” (web:Ps.137.2), then reporting the captors' own demand in quotation, “Sing us one of the songs of Zion!” (web:Ps.137.3), before the exiles' own rhetorical refusal closes the row, “How can we sing Yahweh's song in a foreign land?” (web:Ps.137.4). All 4 verses of this span stay in the communal "we" voice; the row closes where that voice narrows to first-person-singular at web:Ps.137.5.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the captivity scene (137:1-2) from the captors' demand and the refusal (137:3-4) was considered; rejected because both share the same first-person-plural "we" voice with no addressee shift between them, 0 of 4 verses (137:1-4) carry a second-person or first-person-singular form outside the captors' own quoted demand, and 137:4's question is the direct rhetorical answer to 137:3's own demand.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person-plural "we" voice runs unbroken from web:Ps.137.1 through web:Ps.137.4
quoted captors' demand at web:Ps.137.3 ("Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"), answered by the rhetorical question of web:Ps.137.4

edited_rows.rationale: The voice narrows from communal "we" to first-person-singular self-imprecation: “אִֽם אֶשְׁכָּחֵ֥ךְ יְֽרוּשָׁלִָ֗ם” (oshb:Ps.137.5) -- “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.” (web:Ps.137.5) -- continuing “Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I don't remember you, if I don't prefer Jerusalem above my chief joy.” (web:Ps.137.6). Jerusalem is addressed directly by name in apostrophe across both verses, distinct from the preceding "we"-voiced captivity scene and the imprecation that follows: 137:7 opens a fresh second-person imperative addressed to Yahweh against Edom, while 137:8-9 turn to address Babylon directly in the second-person feminine singular.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding this couplet into the following imprecation (137:7-9) was considered, since both continue the psalm's private voice; rejected because 137:5-6 is self-imprecation addressed to Jerusalem by apostrophe, while 137:7 opens a fresh imperative addressed to Yahweh against a third party.

Jerusalem addressed by name in direct apostrophe across web:Ps.137.5-Ps.137.6
